claims.text: Compositionally complex alloys can undergo a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
The proposed transition occurs within 500 K to 800 K.
Temper embrittlement is most pronounced in conventional alloys between 500 K and 800 K.
Compositionally complex alloys resist temper embrittlement.
The relevant behavior can be observed and understood using in-situ TEM during temperature variation.
The proposed material is an FCC compositionally complex alloy with a uniform grain structure.
The alloy will be subjected to temperature variation from 300 K to 1000 K at 5 K/min.
In-situ TEM will be conducted under high-vacuum conditions.
Additional experiments or simulations will mimic practical environmental conditions.
Grain-boundary segregation and dislocation density mediate the response to temperature.
Temperature activates grain-boundary segregation.
Temperature activates dislocation glide.
Grain-boundary segregation and dislocation glide mitigate ductility loss in compositionally complex alloys.
The proposed mechanism reduces the propensity for grain-boundary embrittlement.
The proposed mechanism promotes dislocation mobility.
The compositionally complex alloy will exhibit 20% greater ductility than conventional FCC alloys between 500 K and 800 K.
The predicted ductility increase has a standard deviation of 5%.
Ductility will be measured using the area under the stress–strain curve.
The hypothesis is falsified if the ductility increase is below 15% in the 500 K to 800 K interval.
The hypothesis is falsified if grain-boundary segregation increases above 10% or dislocation density increases above 20%.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts a ductile–brittle–ductile transition while attributing it to resistance to embrittlement and predicting mitigation of ductility loss. It does not explain how a distinct brittle intermediate state can coexist with the proposed mitigation and increased ductility.

Grain-boundary segregation is presented as part of the beneficial mechanism, but an increase in segregation above an arbitrary threshold is treated as falsifying. The direction and amount of segregation required for the proposed benefit are not specified.
